speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We have world-class air and sea ports that connect us to the rest of the world and an extensive public transport system that enables our people to move around efficiently for work and leisure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Ensuring safety is a key focus of our transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We set high safety standards through legislation and regulations and close oversight of our transport operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Our transport operators also employ technology, train their personnel and run safety campaigns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: When they do occur, it is important that we learn from them, identify the causes and take measures to prevent a recurrence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: As these investigations aim to identify lessons and not to ascribe blame, they enable those involved in an incident to freely share information in a truthful manner without any fear of being penalised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Transport Safety Investigations (TSI) Bill will be the single legislation that governs the conduct of safety investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It will facilitate the TSIB's work and enable TSIB investigators to effectively perform their safety functions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Currently, TSIB conducts safety investigations into air and marine incidents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It will standardise the procedures for the conduct of investigations and apply the same set of safeguards on the treatment of information obtained during an investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill states the purposes of the Bill, one of which is for the prevention of future transport occurrences and not for ascribing blame to any person or organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 15 makes clear that TSIB may investigate incidents involving any combination of modes of transport vehicles, and between civilian and military transport vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 16 of the Bill sets out the scope of TSIB's investigations, which include incidents involving civilian aircraft and vessels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: When TSIB has built up its rail accident investigation capabilities, they will also conduct safety investigations into domestic and international railway incidents which happen on or after a date set by the Minister under clause 5.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: When directed by the Minster for Transport, TSIB may also investigate incidents involving certain land transport incidents involving buses, such as those operating under the Land Transport Authority's (LTA's) public bus services contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: As is the case under the existing legislation in the Air Navigation Act, clause 16 of the Bill will continue to allow TSIB to investigate an incident involving only military aircraft engaged in a flying display in Singapore organised by civilians.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 23(5) specifies that these powers are exercisable by TSIB investigators only when and to the extent authorised by the Director of TSIB.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 43 of the Bill prescribes limits on the disclosure of restricted information collected during an investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This limit on disclosure is important in order to encourage the free flow of safety information in transport safety investigations and is also necessary in order to meet international requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Examples of restricted information include witnesses' statements, medical or private information, voice and image recordings and their transcripts, analysis of information and draft final reports.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This clause, however, does not prevent transport regulators and other agencies from conducting their own investigations to obtain similar information directly from the source.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 44 provides that TSIB investigators are not compellable to give any evidence or provide any expert opinion in any proceedings except to a Coroner's inquiry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This reinforces the purpose of the Bill, which is not to ascribe blame to any person or organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Information obtained by TSIB in the course of their investigation is to be used solely for the purpose of improving safety and not by the judicial system whose purpose is for blame or liability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 18 of the Bill specifies that the expenses incurred by TSIB during an investigation is recoverable from the owner or operator, or both, of the transport vehicles involved in the incident.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: To enable the findings and lessons learnt from TSIB's safety investigations to be shared with as many people as possible, clause 20 of the Bill requires TSIB to make their investigation reports publicly available.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 21 of the Bill prevents the TSIB's reports from being used for disciplinary or criminal purposes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Accordingly, the TSIB's draft reports are inadmissible in all Courts and proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Reports of completed investigations are also inadmissible in all Courts and proceedings except a Coroner's inquiry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The work of TSIB is notable for its independence and objectivity, and its focus on preventing future accidents and incidents rather than apportioning blame.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These characteristics allow it to carry out its existing functions effectively through the Air Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) and the Marine Safety Investigation Branch (MSIB).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will allow a greater proportion of transport users to benefit from the robust work of TSIB.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I would like to clarify a point with regard to the recovery of costs and expenses of the investigation, under clause 18 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, I would like to clarify a point with regard to the powers to detain vehicles under clause 30 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The clause states that the director of TSIB has the power to detain a transport vehicle on reasonable grounds, which includes the powers to stop, move and take control of the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The clause also states that the Director must not detain a transport vehicle under this section for longer than is necessary and reasonable to exercise any other powers under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I would like to clarify a point with regard to the general exemptions of the Bill, under clause 47.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The clause states that the Minister may, by order in the Gazette, exempt any person or class of persons or any transport vehicle or class of transport vehicles from all or any provisions of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This mission will improve public safety and should be supported.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I have two queries on the enhanced TSIB and how it will operate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, TSIB investigations and other investigations or proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My first query relates to how TSIB investigations will proceed if there are other agencies or bodies investigating the same incident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I understand it, TSIB's primary concern is safety and recommendations to improve safety.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the same clause rightly recognises that blame or liability may be inferred from its report.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will TSIB's work relate to the work of other investigative agencies?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Let us take a scenario of two marine vessels colliding within Singapore port limits, resulting in deaths.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A Coroner's inquiry or other Inquiry will usually be conducted, which means the Police will likely commence investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under this Bill, TSIB will also be activated to conduct its own investigations into what caused the accident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will TSIB and the Police share their findings with each other, or will they work independently?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there a possibility of conflicting findings being reached by TSIB and other agencies, for example, TSIB may find that there was a mechanical problem in one of the vessels, while the Police may find that the crew was reckless?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does this mean that the Coroner will wait for TSIB to finalise its report before the Coroner reaches his verdict on the likely cause of death?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second point concerns how TSIB will preserve its independence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to clauses 8 and 11 of the Bill, TSIB is to be headed by a Director who will be a public officer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the investigators, clause 23 provides that where an investigation is needed, the Director will appoint either TSIB staff members or consultants as investigators.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, a finding of the factors that contributed to deaths or injuries may encourage lawsuits from victims and lead to reputational and economic damage to big players in the transport industry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate, we can recall the tragic crash 20 years ago of Silkair flight MI 185 over Palembang.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that incident, there was controversy around whether the crash had been caused by deliberate pilot action, or by mechanical or other causes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A lawsuit was brought in Singapore by the families of six victims who refused to reach settlements with Silkair.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court had to consider two conflicting findings from transportation investigation agencies – the Indonesian National Safety Transportation Committee and the United States (US) National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Indonesian agency concluded that the cause of death was unascertainable while the US NTSB found that the crash was likely caused by intentional pilot action.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Eventually, the Court found that the cause was unascertainable and the families lost their cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, if the US NTSB finding had been accepted, Silkair would not have been covered by the applicable Warsaw Conventions to limit payout to each victim to US$75,000 each.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the Silkair incident illustrates that the enormous pressure that may confront the TSIB Director and investigation team when probing such high-stakes incidents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems to me that if we want TSIB to succeed as a credible agency, TSIB must be absolutely fearless in its investigations and not be seen to cower to transport regulators or big business.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, how senior in the Public Service will the Director of TSIB be to have the independence and clout needed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the normal course of events, TSIB would have interviewed the relevant parties in the incident before coming to conclusions in any draft report.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By allowing parties to make representations about the draft report, could this be a window for parties to lobby TSIB to change its findings?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would ask the Minister to clarify the purpose of allowing a person to make representations at this late stage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I have raised several queries and concerns for the Ministry's response.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I certainly hope that the enhanced TSIB will grow into an agency with a solid reputation for independent investigations that will enhance transport safety.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, we pride ourselves as a busy regional and international aviation and maritime hub.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On top of that, our railways see a huge volume of traffic on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While fortunately, accidents involving aircraft, marine craft and railway are not a frequent occurrence in Singapore, the probability of incidences is certainly on the higher side, given the volume of traffic we handle.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To keep this probability low, besides having in place adequate safety measures, it is crucial to ensure all incidences are duly reported.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In doing so, the key is not to lay blame on anyone, but to empower the relevant authorities and personnel to learn from shortcomings and resolve them, so we may prevent them in future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thus, I am pleased to note the significance on incident management and reporting in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When it comes to transport, there is plenty at stake.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In less severe cases, there is some damage and/or loss of property.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In serious accidents, human lives are at stake.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Prevention should remain the focus when it comes to dealing with accidents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not just about looking into how an accident had happened and what could have been done to prevent it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rather, the prevention work that is in place to lower the probability of an accident happening at all is imperative.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the initial staff strength be drawn by transferring some manpower from the Civil Aviation Authority, Maritime and Port Authority, Public Utilities Board and so on?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If so, how many people will be affected by this transfer?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, with a new set up and a new grouping of people in place, how long will it take before TSIB becomes effectively operational?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are we seeking any ad hoc appointments of experts from overseas to help put us on a strong foundation?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There would even be opportunities for TSIB to collaborate with our Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) to work on fire safety matters, as I see it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note in the Bill, it is stated that TSIB may be called upon to render assistance to foreign countries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that "consultants" are referred to in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe this means TSIB recognises that it would have to draw on external expertise to augment its investigation teams.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And on the subject of expertise, it would be ideal if, further down the road, TSIB could set up its own training centre to develop local talents who would be well-versed in dealing with local and even transport occurrences in foreign context.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent years, international media has captured a number of high-profile drone accidents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Amongst them, one of the most serious accidents involved a drone operator who crashed a quadcopter into the grounds of the White House, triggering a security lockdown.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Eventually, the US attorney did not pursue criminal charges against the operator as the incident was determined to be not deliberate as the operator had simply “lost control” of the device.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Indeed, most accidents are not deliberate, so who will be held responsible if damages, casualties, or even fatalities stem from a drone accident?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In July 2014, a drone had narrowly missed colliding with an Airbus A320 as it was taking off from London's Heathrow airport.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Singapore, we have been fortunate to have had no serious accidents involving drones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With technology enthusiasts touting the potential of the use of drones in all sorts of important situations, from delivering parcels to security patrols, it is high time we also looked into safety and incident management for drones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there plans for more incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in the area of data science?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would foresee TSIB working closely with our Defence Science Technology Agency (DSTA), using technology to develop accident prevention devices that can be used by our transport operators.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   On the other hand, in light of the sophistication and frequency of cyberattacks on databases of the Government and public services, we must ensure that security of our data systems is in top form and frequently reviewed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Errors in or deliberate tampering of data can lead to inaccurate information, causing disruption and inconveniences to transport commuters.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the worst scenario, fatal accidents may occur.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would foresee that terrorists could hire hackers to tamper with public transport systems to cause mass accidents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Bureau to prioritise cybersecurity management and cyberhygiene as part of safety management efforts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): I now refer to section 22, Responses to reports of, or containing, safety recommendations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After TSIB has made a recommendation, the party to whom a recommendation is made must give a written response to the Director within a prescribed time after the report was published.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I do have some questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The TSI Bill is a new omnibus Bill that will centralise the conduct of transport safety investigations by TSIB.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What key advantages would such centralisation provide, and has the Ministry studied examples of what have been done overseas?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Australia, for example, has a similar transport safety bureau that only covers the aviation, marine and rail sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there certain specialist knowledge required to investigate public bus accidents, as compared to a normal vehicular accident on our roads?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, the Bill limits the TSIB’s role to investigating only incidents involving buses that are operating under the LTA’s public bus service contracts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Why not extend the powers to cover all types of bus incidents?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With so much innovation disrupting the land transport sector currently, should not TSIB have the powers to step in and investigate major incidents on our public roads that are beyond the public bus contracts?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On that note, new and emerging forms of land transport also do not seem to have been covered under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Clause 16(3) states that subsection (2) – which covers exempt vehicles – does not prevent an investigation of a transport occurrence that involves a Singapore military ship or Singapore military aircraft, if an appropriate authority in the Singapore Armed Forces requests the Director or TSIB to conduct an investigation into the matter.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is my understanding that military and Police vehicles are exempt because otherwise the personnel involved would have to give testimony that may cover national security matters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Minister under what circumstances would the Air Force or Navy request TSIB to investigate an incident involving a military aircraft or a military vessel.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If a request is, indeed, made for TSIB to investigate, some protocol should be put in place to address and safeguard security information relating to the incident or the assets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What about incidents involving Police vehicles or those used by our border control or Civil Defence departments?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill clearly exempts such vessels from investigation by TSIB.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would a similar provision, therefore, be made for these agencies to request TSIB to investigate?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the move to expand the TSIB’s scope into the rail and bus sectors, how does TSIB intend to build its capabilities in investigating such areas?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, how does the Ministry plan to keep the skills of their investigators sharp?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, therefore, necessary that our transport investigators are well-trained and have the mandate to be flexible enough to investigate all possible modes of transport across the air, land and sea sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern is with the deep specialisation of these specialist investigators and how to upkeep the currency of their knowledge and skillsets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Like Ms Sylvia Lim who spoke earlier, I hope that TSIB will one day be a highly regarded transport safety investigation agency that we can all be proud of.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This arena of transport safety investigations is very specialised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is a fairly unique process; it has been tested in practice; it has an international application.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It arose really from our obligations under some international treaties, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This Bill brings together the work that has been already ongoing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have been doing the work already but this Bill will facilitate that work.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It brings it together under one legislative framework, and it enables the investigators to effectively perform their safety functions, improve transport safety, and be in accord with international practices as well as our international agreements under one legislative framework.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Many countries have a similar multi-modal transport investigation agency – Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, the US.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Having a multi-modal transport safety investigation agency allows the cross-sharing of best practices and resources.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While there is a need for domain-specific industry experience, engineering experience, safety operation experience, there is a significant amount of cross-sharing in terms of legal practices, cross-border issues, and how one interfaces with other Government agencies, among other things.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there is a need for deep specialisation – aviation experts, maritime experts, subsequently rail experts.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But there is also a need to bring them together administratively, and the experience from overseas shows that this works.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It also allows the deepening of the investigation expertise, for example, in the human and system factors.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: TSIB is staffed with very experienced and competent investigators, currently with aviation and maritime industry experience.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, this industry experience is something very significant.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While they have been in industry, they have had the experience of operating some of these safety issues, of designing safety policies within their agency, within their commercial organisation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, they bring to bear, when they come and work under TSIB, all of those years of experience.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The director has 20 years of experience and is a fairly senior person, and it is that level of expertise that we will need to have.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some of the Members asked about training and capability development.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The investigators attend both local as well as foreign training courses to update their knowledge of transport systems, to sharpen their investigation capabilities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the training is ongoing; it is not just merely at the point of entry at TSIB.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, we are able to and have brought in both volunteer investigators as well as appointed overseas experts, depending on the nature of the incident and the case that is being investigated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A whole series of resources will be brought together, depending on what is needed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The number of people, however, that we need here in Singapore in order to do this, while they are very talented and have deep expertise, is probably not a number that will justify a single training centre.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we are not looking to do this by transferring people across different parts of the Government because these types of capabilities will be needed in other agencies and in other entities, because there is an ongoing need for investigations, for disciplinary processes, enforcement and regulations, and so forth.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we want to build up a separate arm of capability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The objective of TSIB is really just to focus on the safety standards, looking at the causes, drawing safety lessons, preventing recurrence.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The question was raised about why not all buses, why not all major incidents?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, again, I would reiterate, there are plenty of other organisations and agencies that can investigate – the Police; LTA itself can conduct an investigation; the Minister for Transport can also convene committees and Commissions of Inquiry, for instance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, by constituting TSIB, it is not that all investigations will only happen under the remit of TSIB.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is a very specific and particular type of investigation that will happen under TSIB, and all the other agencies that can continue to investigate incidents and systems will continue to have that opportunity to do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The reason why we have looked at the provisions specifically for LTA-contracted bus services, firstly, it is about the systems associated with it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You need something which is a fairly complex system to begin with organisationally to justify this type of investigation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But in this case, we wanted something, apart from LTA, to investigate LTA-contracted services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This independent assessment of safety issues and recommendations would run in parallel to any potential Traffic Police investigation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, as part of that international agreement, we have had to then put in that exemption clause.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we do have jurisdiction to investigate the occurrences between one of these exempted vehicles and one which is not, that is, one which is a civilian vehicle.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One of the Members asked about what are the circumstances in which the SAF would request TSIB to conduct an investigation into a transport occurrence that involves a Singapore military ship or Singapore military aircraft.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think that is an issue for them to answer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: TSIB is available as a pool of resources and expertise that are there, so, if there is a need for this particular type of safety investigation and we are resourced to be called upon by the SAF.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If the investigation involves information that is relevant for national security, there are already protocols in place, and that came out of the experience that the Air Accident Investigation Bureau had, working together with the Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, protocols have been developed and they will extend across all these different interagency boundaries to deal with issues around sensitive information, to allow these investigations to proceed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Members brought up the issue of the exemption that the Minister for Transport can order through the Gazette.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This will only be exercised in highly exceptional cases and it will not be taken lightly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This exemption arises from the fact that there is an international requirement for the provisions of the Bill, which provide TSIB with a significant amount of powers and require the reports to be made public, and we do want to make sure that when it is necessary from a national interest, that certain vehicles can be exempted from those provisions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It will be done through an order in the Gazette and will not be taken lightly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Each investigation takes approximately one year to complete.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no transfer of investigations from other agencies, and there will not be as these new domains are investigated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the detention of vehicles under clause 30, which empowers the Director to detain a transport vehicle for the reasons given.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no expressed cap on the duration of detention.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, TSIB will be mindful not to detain these vehicles for longer than necessary.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: With respect to the issue of costs, today already, air incident investigation costs and expenses are recovered from owners and operators whose aircraft are the subject of investigations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, clause 18 is really looking for parity across a number of domains just to make sure that the same approach and same treatment are applied.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The examples of the types of costs were asked, for example, the cost of conducting specialised tests, recovering and storing the wreckage as well as administrative and operational overheads of conducting the investigation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, in particular, asked about the information that will be obtained by TSIB in the course of investigation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the requirement is that the information is used solely for the purpose of improving transport safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is why the Bill is crafted in the way it is, in order to maintain that opportunity to have a free flow of information without the fear that the persons giving that information will be penalised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, in order to do so, the TSIB staff, as well as former staff who are involved need to be distanced from judicial proceedings.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They cannot be compelled to give evidence in civil or criminal proceedings related to the incident.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Further to that, some information, such as onboard recording information, cannot be disclosed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The final part of this component is that the investigation report is inadmissible as evidence in Courts and proceedings, with the exception of the coroner's inquiry, and that is to stay consistent with the fundamental purpose of these transport safety investigations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The reason why the coroner's inquiry has an exception made for it is because the purpose of the coroner's inquiry is to determine the cause and circumstances connected with the death without necessarily framing a finding as to determining a question of criminal, civil or disciplinary liability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, this barrier against disclosure is not absolute.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But ultimately, it is the coroner's prerogative to decide whether it is necessary to wait for the conclusion of the TSIB investigation before making a decision about the cause of death, the verdict on the cause of death.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is not under TSIB's remit, it will be up to the coroner to decide, and the coroner will be aware that this investigation is happening and the coroner will have to make that decision.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are issues with respect to the coordination of multiple investigations from multiple agencies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the agencies involved have developed a standard operating procedure to make sure that they adhere to their own regulatory framework as well as to allow the investigation to proceed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, during the course of the investigation, TSIB will engage with the parties concerned to deliberate the information collected to analyse the contributing factors and to try to make some preliminary recommendations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But ultimately, the drafting of the report is by TSIB.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: TSIB has to take full responsibility for those recommendations and stand by them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, where there is, for example, conflicting information that is coming in, TSIB has to make the decision about what would be their recommendations and justify these in their report.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am sure there will be an attempt to put across vested interests and lobbying and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it is precisely because of that, that we need to ensure that there are protections for the Director of TSIB and the officers of TSIB to have that independence when they issue their recommendations in their final report.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked about the penalty for failing to respond to safety recommendations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not as a punitive penalty for a safety lapse for an incident, which is a matter not for TSIB to determine, but for the Police or for the agencies or the regulators to investigate and determine as needed.
